pos: n. (proper name; Cyrus's treasurer, and a Persian official of Artaxerxes' reign)
etymology: Persian, meaning given by Mithras — a theophoric name formed on the Persian deity Mithra. The Greek form of the same name is Mithridates.
biblical_def: Mithredath is named twice, of two Persian officials. The first is the man who handed back the temple vessels: “Even those did Cyrus king of Persia bring forth by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah” (Ezra 1:8). Nebuchadnezzar had carried the vessels of the house of the LORD into the house of his gods (Ezra 1:7); seventy years later a Persian treasurer counted them out again, five thousand four hundred pieces of gold and silver, into the hands of a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:11). The second Mithredath writes to Artaxerxes to stop the rebuilding (Ezra 4:7). The Authorized Version prints the name twice. The dictionary notes what the first verse demonstrates. God used a pagan emperor, named by Isaiah a hundred and fifty years before he was born, and a treasurer named after a Persian god, to restore the vessels of His own worship. Providence does not require its instruments to be believers. The vessels went out under judgment and came back by inventory, counted by a man whose name honoured Mithras.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The return under Cyrus is routinely explained as ordinary Persian imperial policy toward subject religions, which it also was. That explanation is not wrong; it is incomplete. Isaiah had named Cyrus by name and called him the LORD's shepherd and His anointed long before, and Ezra 1:1 says the LORD stirred up his spirit. Secondary causes are real and are not the first cause.

pos: n. (a Babylonian court title, borne by Nergalsharezer at the fall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Babylonian rab-mugi, chief officer; the element rab means chief, as in Rabsaris and Rabshakeh. The Authorized Version prints it as a name beside Nergalsharezer.
biblical_def: The word appears twice, in the account of Jerusalem's fall: “And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon” (Jeremiah 39:3), and again at Jeremiah 39:13. Rab is the Babylonian word for chief, as in Rabsaris, chief of the eunuchs, and Rabshakeh, chief cupbearer; Rabmag is a title of high office. The Authorized Version prints it beside the man's name, and the dictionary follows the Authorized reading. What matters is what these officers did next: “Even they sent, and took Jeremiah out of the court of the prison, and committed him unto Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan, that he should carry him home: so he dwelt among the people” (Jeremiah 39:14). The men who sacked the city released the prophet his own countrymen had put in a dungeon. Forty years of preaching had got him beaten and imprisoned in Jerusalem; the Babylonian high command gave him his liberty and let him choose where to live.

pos: n. (a precinct or colonnade on the west side of the temple, guarded by the porters)
etymology: Hebrew Parbar, of uncertain meaning; probably a precinct, suburb, or open colonnade. 2 Kings 23:11 has a related form rendered the suburbs.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice in one verse, in the roster of the temple gatekeepers: “At Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar” (1 Chronicles 26:18). The Authorized Version keeps the Hebrew word untranslated because its sense is not certain; it is a precinct or colonnade on the west side of the temple, and David's arrangement posted six Levites there. The chapter is the muster-roll of the porters, and it describes an ordered guard: “Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 26:12). The dictionary notes two things. The office of porter was a ministry — the verse says so, to minister in the house of the LORD — and the men who held it were assigned by lot, east, north, south, and west, with names and numbers recorded. And the psalmist, who was of their company, wrote the verse that has honoured them ever since: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psalm 84:10).

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of temple porters who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Shobay, of uncertain meaning, possibly from a root for returning or for taking captive.
biblical_def: Shobai heads one of the six porter families in the register of the return: “The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine” (Ezra 2:42). Nehemiah's copy of the same register gives a hundred thirty and eight (Nehemiah 7:45). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the single-digit difference, which is the sort of thing a careless reader calls an error and a careful one calls a separate count: Ezra's list and Nehemiah's differ in several totals, exactly as two tallies of a migrating population taken at different moments would. Neither writer edits the other to agree. What the register records is more striking than the arithmetic. A hundred and thirty-nine men whose fathers had kept the gates of a temple that had been burned seventy years earlier came back from Babylon to keep the gates of a temple not yet rebuilt. They returned to an office before there was a house to exercise it in.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The numerical differences between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are a standing exhibit for those who deny inerrancy. They are two registers of a population in motion, taken at different points, and neither claims to be a copy of the other. Inerrancy is a claim about what the text asserts, and neither text asserts that its total is the other's.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the tenacity of office. Shobai's family had not kept a temple gate in seventy years, and they came back from a settled life in Babylon to resume a duty whose building was rubble. Faith reckons an office that God appointed to be still standing.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Padon, probably from padah, to ransom or redeem — the verb used of the redemption of the firstborn.
biblical_def: Padon appears twice, in the two copies of one register: “The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon” (Ezra 2:44), with Nehemiah 7:47. His family belonged to the Nethinim — the given ones, the temple servants whose descent Joshua traced to the Gibeonites made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. The Authorized Version uses the name twice and says nothing else. The dictionary notes the name's root, which is padah, to redeem by paying a price: the verb of Exodus 13:13, every firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem, and of Psalm 130:8, he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities. A family of temple servants, descended from a people spared by a treaty, bearing a name built on the word for ransom, went up out of Babylon to serve in the house of God. Scripture lists them with the priests and the Levites and the singers and the porters, by name and by household, which is the point: the lowest order of temple service was registered as carefully as the highest.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite settler in Jerusalem, and a head of priests)
etymology: Hebrew Sallay, probably from salal, to lift up or cast up a highway. Nehemiah 12:7 gives Sallu as an alternative form.
biblical_def: The name belongs to two men of the restoration. The first is a Benjamite counted among those who settled in the rebuilt city: “And after him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight” (Nehemiah 11:8). The second is a priestly house: “Of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber” (Nehemiah 12:20), with the margin at Nehemiah 12:7 noting Sallu: or, Sallai. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the chapter these verses sit in. Nehemiah 11 is the register of the men who agreed to live in Jerusalem, and the chapter opens by explaining the arrangement: the rulers dwelt there, and the people cast lots to bring one of ten to dwell in the holy city, and they blessed the men that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem. The city was rebuilt, under-populated, exposed, and expensive to live in. Nine hundred and twenty-eight Benjamites went. Scripture blesses men who volunteer for the hard post and writes their names down, and Sallai is in the list because he was one of them.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Shalmay, probably from shalam, to be complete or to requite. The Authorized Version's margin at Ezra 2:46 records the variant Shamlai.
biblical_def: Shalmai heads a Nethinim family in the register of the return: “The children of Hagab, the children of Shalmai, the children of Hanan” (Ezra 2:46), with the parallel at Nehemiah 7:48. The Authorized Version uses the name twice, and its margin at Ezra 2:46 preserves the alternative reading Shamlai, a transposition of two consonants. The dictionary notes the translators' practice, because it is a model of how a faithful translation handles a textual variant: print the reading, note the alternative, explain nothing away. Nothing in Christian doctrine depends on whether a Nethinim family head was called Shalmai or Shamlai, and the Authorized Version does not pretend otherwise. What the verse establishes is the care of the record. Thirty-five Nethinim families are named in Ezra 2, men whose work was carrying wood and water for the temple, and every household head is listed by name. A government counts taxpayers; this register counts servants. The God who numbers the hairs of the head had the names of the temple's lowest servants written into His book.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite musician appointed by David to the second degree)
etymology: Hebrew Miqneyahu, probably meaning possession of Jehovah, from miqneh, possession or cattle, and the divine name.
biblical_def: Mikneiah is named twice, both in the chapter where David brings up the ark the second time and appoints the Levites to sing: “And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel... and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters” (1 Chronicles 15:18), and then at his post: “And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1 Chronicles 15:21). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the order David established: “And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy” (1 Chronicles 15:16). This is the chapter in which worship is reorganised after the disaster of Uzza — the ark carried by Levites, on their shoulders, as the law required, after the first attempt had followed Philistine practice and a man had died. Mikneiah's name means possession of Jehovah, and he took his harp to a post the Levites held because the second attempt was made God's way.

corruption_summary: 1 Chronicles 15 is cited to license whatever a congregation likes in worship; the chapter exists because the first attempt was not after the due order.
corruption_paragraphs: The harps and cymbals of 1 Chronicles 15 are a favourite warrant for treating corporate worship as a matter of free arrangement. The chapter is in fact the strongest Old Testament case for the opposite. David says plainly why the first attempt killed a man: because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:13). The cart was Philistine; the shoulders of the Levites were commanded.

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship. What God commands in corporate worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted there. David did not reduce the joy — the voice was lifted up with joy, the instruments sounded, the men were appointed to excel — he submitted the manner to the word.

pos: n. (proper name; an Ephraimite father, and a priestly ancestor in Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Meshillemoth, a plural form from shalam, to requite — meaning recompenses or retributions.
biblical_def: The name belongs to two men. The first stands behind one of the most remarkable acts of mercy in the Old Testament: “Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, and Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against them that came from the war” (2 Chronicles 28:12). Israel had taken two hundred thousand captives from Judah; the prophet Oded met the army and told them to send them home; and four named Ephraimites stood in the road and stopped their own victorious troops. What they then did is in the next verses — they clothed the naked captives, shod them, fed them, anointed them, carried the feeble on asses, and brought them to Jericho. The second Meshillemoth is a priestly ancestor at Nehemiah 11:13. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the word's meaning: recompenses. Four men whose fathers' names spoke of requital gave their enemies food and clothing, which is the law's own instruction and the apostle's: if thine enemy hunger, feed him.

corruption_paragraphs: The reading to resist treats 2 Chronicles 28 as an anomaly, a flash of humanitarian instinct in an otherwise brutal record. It is nothing of the kind. A prophet spoke, four named men obeyed, and the law they obeyed was already written: Proverbs 25:21, if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat. The Old Testament ethic toward enemies is not what it is commonly assumed to be.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courage of standing against one's own side. Four heads of Ephraim stood up against an army of their own countrymen returning in triumph, and made them give back the spoil. That is harder than opposing an enemy, and Scripture names the four men who did it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Meshillemoth, recompenses, from shalam; father of Berechiah, one of the four Ephraimites who freed Judah's captives.

pos: n. (proper name; father of one of David's mighty men, and a son of Obededom)
etymology: Hebrew Sakar, from sakar, hire, wages, or reward — the word of Genesis 15:1, I am thy exceeding great reward.
biblical_def: The name belongs to two men. The first is the father of a mighty man: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35), with the margin offering or, Sharar for the parallel in Samuel. The second is a temple porter: “Moreover the sons of Obededom were, Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, and Sacar the fourth, and Nethaneel the fifth” (1 Chronicles 26:4). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the household the second Sacar belonged to, because the Chronicler comments on it and rarely comments on anything. Obededom is the man in whose house the ark lodged three months after Uzza died, and the LORD blessed his household; and when the Chronicler lists his eight sons and their sons, sixty-two men of the gatekeeping families, he explains it in four words: “Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peulthai the eighth: for God blessed him” (1 Chronicles 26:5). Sacar's name means wages, and he was one of the wages God paid a man who had sheltered the ark.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives no entry for Sacar; the name belongs to the father of one of David's mighty men and to the fourth son of Obededom.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The blessing on Obededom's house is a favourite prosperity text, pressed into a transaction: shelter the ark, receive increase. The Chronicler is making a narrower point. God had just struck Uzza for touching the ark, and Israel was afraid of it; Obededom took it in, and God blessed him, so that the whole nation could see the ark was a blessing to those who received it rightly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the word Sacar. Sakar is reward, and Genesis 15:1 says to Abram, I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward. The reward of hosting God's presence is God's presence; the sons and the office came with it.
